keys.mpf_note_1:
This is the flow and depth inside an infinitely long pipe.
Getting the flow into the pipe may require significantly higher headwater depth. Add at least 1.5 times the velocity head to get the headwater depth or see my 2-minute tutorial for standard culvert headwater calculations using HY-8.

keys.mphl_note_1:
For an open inlet (culvert) condition, it is necessary to check for inlet control conditions.
1. The upstream HGL cannot be lower than the upstream normal depth flow elevation (or lower than the pipe!).
2. The headwater of a culvert is better represented by the upstream EGL than the upstream HGL.
3. See my 2-minute tutorial for simple standard culvert headwater calculations using HY-8.

keys.mtc_note_1: <dl><dt>Automated rock size and roughness design iteration</dt><dd>Choose a roughness radio button (BB recommended) and a design rock size radio button (Isbash recommended). Fine-tune depth and rock size safety factor to get your desired flow with an even rock size. Every time you change any input value, the following iteration cycle happens: 1. Roughness is calculated from design rock size. 2. The requested roughness calculation is copied to input roughness. 3. Channel flow and required rock size are calculated. 4. Design rock size is adjusted. 5. Repeat until error in the design rock size is very small.</dd><dt>Basic calculator (no iteration)</dt><dd>Enter your desired roughness value. Ignore the design rock size input area.</dd></dl>
keys.mtc_note_2_def: High velocity implies high specific energy from an available drop. That energy can be lost quickly at expansions, bends, or obstructions. Verify that this is reasonable for the site.
keys.ws_main_title: Free Online Simple Broad-crested Weir Flow Calculator
keys.wi_main_title: Free Online Segmented, Variable Depth, Irregular Weir Flow Calculator
keys.wi_notes_we_def: q = if (length = 0) then 0 else if (slope=0) then cw*length*d<sub>0</sub><sup>1.5</sup> else cw/(2.5*slope) * (d<sub>0</sub><sup>2.5</sup> - d<sub>1</sub><sup>2.5</sup>) where d<sub>1</sub> and d<sub>0</sub> are always positive or zero
keys.or_diameter: Diameter or height, D ?
keys.or_width: Width, W ?
keys.or_invert: Invert elevation ?
keys.or_regime_warn: Warning: headwater below crown — not orifice regime
keys.or_regime_twe_above_hwe: Warning: tailwater (TWE) above headwater (HWE) — check inputs
keys.or_notes_1_def: Q = C<sub>d</sub> × A × √(2gh). For free outfall: h = HWE − centroid. For submerged flow (TWE above invert): h = HWE − TWE.
keys.or_notes_2_def: Orifice flow equations apply when the headwater surface is above the crown (top) of the opening. When headwater is below the crown, use a weir equation instead.
keys.or_notes_3_def: Cd ranges from about 0.60–0.65 for sharp-edged orifices. Rounded or re-entrant inlets use different values. See the Engineering Toolbox or the HEC-RAS Hydraulic Reference Manual for guidance.
keys.or_notes_4_def: When TWE is above the opening invert, this calculator automatically applies the submerged orifice equation using h = HWE − TWE. When TWE is at or below the invert, free outfall is assumed and h = HWE − centroid.
keys.mhp_km: Minor loss coefficient, km ?
keys.mhp_nu: Kinematic viscosity, ν ?
keys.mhp_vel_low: Velocity low - risk of sedimentation and air entrainment.
keys.mhp_vel_high: Velocity high - risk of water hammer and high point (minor) losses.
keys.mhp_notes_1_def: Total penstock loss h<sub>L</sub> = h<sub>f</sub> + h<sub>m</sub>, where h<sub>f</sub> = f(L/D)(v²/2g) is Darcy-Weisbach friction loss and h<sub>m</sub> = k<sub>m</sub>·v²/2g covers entrance, bends, and valves. Net head H<sub>net</sub> = H<sub>gross</sub> − h<sub>L</sub>.
keys.mhp_notes_2_def: Check that velocity is reasonable for the available drop and pipe cost. Very low velocity may indicate oversizing; very high velocity can increase friction losses and water hammer risk.
keys.mhp_notes_3_def: Penstock losses below 10% of gross head are generally economic. The optimal trade-off between pipe cost and lost power often falls around 4–6% for high-value electricity sites.
keys.mhp_notes_4_def: These losses occur at pipe junctions, entrances, bends, and valves — the term “minor” is conventional but misleading; in a short penstock they can equal or exceed friction losses. Typical k values: sharp intake entrance 0.5, each 45° bend 0.2–0.3, gate valve (fully open) 0.1, butterfly valve 0.2. Sum all fittings for the total k<sub>m</sub>. Default 1.5 assumes one entrance and two bends.
keys.mhp_notes_5_def: Typical absolute roughness: steel (new) 0.046 mm, steel (used) 0.15 mm, HDPE 0.003 mm, PVC/uPVC 0.0015 mm, concrete 0.3–3 mm. HDPE is common for small micro-hydro penstocks.
keys.mhp_notes_6_def: Typical plant efficiency η ranges from 0.70 to 0.85 for Pelton and cross-flow turbines common in micro-hydro. Use 0.75 as a conservative first estimate.
keys.mhp_notes_7_def: Annual energy assumes continuous full-flow operation (8760 hours/year). Actual production will be lower due to seasonal flow variation, maintenance downtime, and load factor.
keys.odt_main_title: Free Online Orifice Drain Time Calculator — Pond, Basin, or Tank
keys.odt_main_desc: Pond or Basin Orifice Drain Time — Conic Volume Method
keys.odt_h1_elev: Starting WSE ?
keys.odt_a_ending: Ending area, A2 ?
keys.odt_h2_warn: Warning: ending elevation at or below orifice top (centroid + D/2)
keys.odt_d: Orifice D ?
keys.odt_w: Orifice width, W ?
keys.odt_notes_1_def: t = √H<sub>1</sub> / (C<sub>d</sub> A<sub>or</sub> √(2g)) × (2A<sub>x</sub>/5 + 8√(A<sub>x</sub>A<sub>0</sub>)/15 + 16A<sub>0</sub>/15) gives drain time from head H to the orifice. Drain time = t(H<sub>1</sub>,A<sub>1</sub>,A<sub>0</sub>) − t(H<sub>2</sub>,A<sub>2</sub>,A<sub>0</sub>), where H<sub>1</sub> = starting elevation − orifice elevation, H<sub>2</sub> = ending elevation − orifice elevation.
keys.odt_notes_2_def: The conic volume method models the pond or basin as a conic section between the starting area A<sub>1</sub> at the initial water surface and the area A<sub>0</sub> at the orifice centroid elevation. A<sub>2</sub>, the pond area at the ending elevation, is interpolated from A<sub>1</sub> and A<sub>0</sub> using the conic section model. Drain time from starting to ending elevation equals total drain time from H<sub>1</sub> to orifice minus remaining drain time from H<sub>2</sub> to orifice.
keys.odt_h1: Starting head, H1 ?
keys.irr_main_title: Free Online Irrigation Flow Measurement Calculators
keys.irr_main_desc: Irrigation Flow Measurement — Weirs and Orifices
keys.irr_intro_html: Weirs and orifices are the standard field tools for measuring water flow in irrigation systems. Select the calculator that matches your structure:
keys.irr_card_weir_uniform_desc: Measure flow over a diversion dam crest, check structure, or weir board. Enter weir length and headwater depth above the crest.
keys.irr_card_weir_irregular_desc: Use when the weir crest is not a single uniform elevation — natural spillways, drop structures with varying width, or multi-section control structures.
keys.irr_card_orifice_desc: Measure flow through a sluice gate, pipe turnout, or culvert opening. Handles both free outfall and submerged (tailwater) conditions automatically.
keys.irr_card_canal_desc: Design or check an irrigation canal using Manning's formula. Use the Trapezoidal calculator for new channels; the Irregular calculator for existing natural or constructed sections.
keys.irr_card_drip_desc: Calculate application rate, distribution uniformity, lateral flow, zone flow, and runtime for a drip or sprinkler irrigation system. Enter emitter flow, emitter spacing, and target depth.
keys.irr_card_seepage_desc: Estimate seepage loss from a canal reach using inflow and outflow measurements. Compute conveyance efficiency and annual water loss to help prioritize lining investments.
keys.irr_quickref_html:
Quick Reference

Diversion dam or check structure
Measure headwater depth above the weir crest. Use Weir Flow Simple for a uniform crest, or Weir Flow Irregular for a profiled or stepped crest.
Headgate or pipe turnout
Measure headwater elevation and tailwater elevation (or invert if freely discharging). Use Orifice Flow. For a circular pipe, D = pipe diameter; for a rectangular gate, enter width W and height D.
Reservoir or pond drain time
Use Orifice Drain Time to estimate how long it takes to lower a pond or reservoir through a bottom orifice — useful for irrigation storage planning.
Field standards
Weir and orifice flow equations used here match USBR Water Measurement Manual (3rd ed.) procedures commonly required by water masters and irrigation districts.
keys.ds_main_title: Free Online Drip/Sprinkler Irrigation Application Rate Calculator
keys.ds_notes_1_def: PR = q / A<sub>e</sub>, where A<sub>e</sub> = S<sub>e</sub> × S<sub>l</sub> is the area served by each emitter. A lower application rate gives more time for infiltration — important on heavy soils or sloped fields.
keys.ds_notes_2_def: Runtime = target depth ÷ application rate. On sloping or compacted soil, split the runtime into two or three shorter cycles with rest periods between them to avoid surface runoff.
keys.cs_main_title: Free Online Canal Seepage Loss and Conveyance Efficiency Calculator
keys.cs_main_desc: Canal Seepage Loss & Conveyance Efficiency — Inflow-Outflow Method
keys.cs_Ec_target: Lining target, Ec,target ?
keys.cs_payback_years: Payback period ?
keys.cs_notes_1_def: The inflow-outflow method estimates seepage by measuring flow at the head and tail of a canal reach: Q<sub>loss</sub> = Q<sub>in</sub> − Q<sub>out</sub>. Conveyance efficiency E<sub>c</sub> = Q<sub>out</sub> / Q<sub>in</sub>. Annual volume assumes continuous full-flow operation; actual loss is lower for seasonal or part-flow canals.
keys.cs_notes_2_def: Typical unlined earthen canals: E<sub>c</sub> = 60–80%. Well-maintained earthen canals: 75–85%. Concrete-lined canals: 90–98%. Seepage losses above 30% of inflow often justify a lining investment. (USBR, FAO)
keys.cs_notes_3_def: Enter water value and lining cost in any consistent currency. Lining area = reach length × wetted perimeter — the wetted perimeter of the canal cross-section at the measured flow depth (bottom width plus both wetted slopes). Annual value recovered assumes the lined canal achieves the target E<sub>c</sub> continuously. Actual payback will be longer for seasonal canals or if the lining does not reach the target efficiency.
keys.cs_notes_4_def: USBR Water Measurement Manual, 3rd ed. (2001). FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 57 (1999).

keys.about_body_html:
Mission

HawsEDC Engineering Calculators exist to serve engineers and field workers around the world — especially those working in water-scarce, low-resource, or underserved regions. These tools are part of a broader humanitarian mission: to tell every human being in the most practical and effective way possible that they are loved and cherished forever, that they have nothing to fear, and that they are not going to ruin everything.

The calculators are the vehicle. The destination is a world free of suffering.

Open Source License

All code is released under the GNU General Public License v3.0 or later — free as in freedom. You may use, study, modify, and redistribute the code under the same terms.

Copyright © 2009–2026 Thomas Gail Haws.

Source Code

The full source code is publicly available on Bitbucket:

bitbucket.org/hawstom/engcalcs

You can browse the code, file issues, or fork the repository there.

Contributing

Pull requests are welcome. Ways to contribute:

  • Translations — improve or add a language. Open a pull request with changes to the relevant lib/lang.ec.??.php file.
  • Bug reports — use the feedback form on any calculator page, or file an issue on Bitbucket.
  • New calculators — ideas for hydraulic engineering tools that serve field workers and irrigation practitioners are especially welcome. See the CLAUDE.md developer guide in the repository.
  • Hosting — if you can mirror these calculators for a region with limited connectivity, please get in touch.

Offline Use

These calculators work as a Progressive Web App (PWA). Visit any calculator page while connected, and your browser will cache all the calculators automatically. After that, all calculators work offline — no internet required.

On Android or iOS, use your browser's "Add to Home Screen" option to install EngCalcs as an app on your device. On desktop, look for the install icon in your browser's address bar.

You can also save any individual calculator using your browser's "Save as…" menu for one-off offline use.

Contact

Tom Haws — hydraulic engineer and author of these calculators.
Use the feedback form on any calculator page, or reach the source code at Bitbucket.

keys.rc_main_title: Free Online Rock Chute Design Calculator — Robinson (1998)
keys.rc_main_desc: Rock Chute Riprap Sizing — Robinson, Rice & Kadavy (1998)
keys.rc_qt: Total unit discharge, qt ?
keys.rc_sg: Rock specific gravity, sg ?
keys.rc_SD: Gradation SD = D84.1/D50 ?
keys.rc_yn: Normal depth in inlet channel, yn ?
keys.rc_D50: Required median rock size, D50 ?
keys.rc_apron_length: Outlet apron length (15 × D50) ?
keys.rc_Vm: Velocity through rock mantle, Vm ?
keys.rc_d: Flow depth above riprap surface, d
keys.rc_Hp: Inlet weir head, Hp ?
keys.rc_pond_warn: ⚠ Hp ≤ yn — no ponding — check inlet for erosion
keys.rc_eq_warn_low: Warning: S0 < 0.02 — below Robinson validation range
keys.rc_eq_warn_high: Warning: S0 > 0.40 — above Robinson validation range
keys.rc_notes_1_def: Robinson, Rice & Kadavy (1998) developed two empirical equations for median riprap size D<sub>50</sub> based on chute slope and unit discharge. Equation 1 applies for mild slopes (S<sub>0</sub> < 0.10); Equation 2 applies for steep slopes (0.10 ≤ S<sub>0</sub> ≤ 0.40). Both equations require q<sub>t</sub> in m²/s and return D<sub>50</sub> in mm. The validated range is 0.02 ≤ S<sub>0</sub> ≤ 0.40.
keys.rc_notes_2_def: q<sub>t</sub> is the total unit discharge at the chute crest (total flow per unit width). For a channel of bottom width B carrying total flow Q, approximate q<sub>t</sub> ≈ Q / B, or compute it from the critical-depth condition at the chute inlet.
keys.rc_notes_3_def: A fraction of the total flow moves through the pores of the rock riprap (mantle flow q<sub>m</sub>); the remainder flows over the rock surface (q<sub>s</sub> = q<sub>t</sub> − q<sub>m</sub>). The flow depth d is computed from Manning’s equation applied to the surface flow q<sub>s</sub> using the chute roughness n. Default porosity n<sub>p</sub> = 0.45 is typical for angular crushed rock.
keys.rc_notes_5_def: The equations were developed using a D<sub>50</sub> range of 15 mm to 278 mm. Results outside this range are extrapolated and should be used with additional engineering judgement.
keys.rc_notes_6_def: The elevation of the top of riprap in the outlet reach should be at or below the downstream channel bed elevation. If it is higher, the outlet rock will be unstable.
keys.rc_notes_7_def: When the normal depth in the inlet channel is less than the weir head (H<sub>p</sub>) required to pass q<sub>t</sub>, restricted flow or ponding occurs upstream of the inlet apron. This is generally acceptable — ponding reduces velocity and prevents erosion upstream. To check: use a weir flow calculator to find H<sub>p</sub> for the given q<sub>t</sub> and crest width, and compare it to the inlet channel normal depth. If H<sub>p</sub> exceeds normal depth, ponding will occur.
keys.rc_notes_4_def: Robinson, K.M., Rice, C.E., and Kadavy, K.C. (1998). “Design of rock chutes.” Transactions of the ASAE, 41(3), 621–626. USDA ARS also publishes an Excel spreadsheet based on the same method.
keys.ip_main_title: Free Online Irrigation Pressure & Distribution Uniformity Calculator
keys.ip_main_desc: Test Branch Pressure and Uniformity Estimate
keys.ip_x: Emitter discharge exponent, x ?
keys.ip_is_lateral: Lat. ?
keys.ip_count: Emitters ?
keys.ip_km: Km ?
keys.ip_elev_ds: DS Elev. ?
keys.ip_elev_ds_missing_warn: Last emitter elevation (last row) was left blank and defaulted to flat — enter it for an accurate result ⚠
keys.ip_hl: Hl ?
keys.ip_pressure_warn: Low/negative pressure — check for subatmospheric conditions
keys.ip_q_supply: Test path supply flow, Qsupply ?
keys.ip_dp_avg: Est. Δpressure, avg. vs. test lateral ?
keys.ip_q_avg_field: Est. field-average emitter flow, qavg,field ?
keys.ip_du_estimate: Uniformity check, qlast/qavg,field ?
keys.ip_worst_case_warn: Test emitter pressure is at or above supply pressure — this path is not likely your worst-case lateral. Check for a more remote or higher-friction lateral, or an elevation profile that better represents the actual worst case.
keys.ip_q_ratio: Last emitter flow vs. design flow, qlast/qdesign ?
keys.ip_no_solution: No solution: required supply pressure exceeds the entered supply pressure. Increase supply pressure, reduce demand, or use a larger pipe.
keys.ip_notes_1_def: Guesses the pressure at the last (most remote) emitter, then marches the Energy Grade Line back toward the supply, reach by reach, adding friction and minor losses along the way. Elevation and velocity head are backed out at each node to report the actual pressure there. The guessed far-end pressure is adjusted (bisection) until the computed required supply pressure matches the entered supply pressure — the same closed-loop problem addressed by the pipe-flow solver on the Manning Pipe Flow calculator, extended to a branching network.
keys.ip_notes_2_def: Each row is one reach along the single hydraulically worst path (the test path) from the supply to the last emitter. A Main reach only passes flow to laterals not on the test path, so its draw is a flat multiplication (design flow × the reach’s total emitter count) — no local pressure sensitivity. The main is a shared trunk pipe, so the reach right at the test lateral’s own takeoff must include not just laterals between its own endpoints but also any laterals still further down the main beyond that takeoff, or sharing the same junction (e.g. an opposite-side lateral) — their flow travels through that same reach before splitting off, whether or not they appear anywhere else in this table. A Lateral reach is a segment of the test lateral itself: emitter discharge is computed from the actual local pressure via q = k·H<sup>x</sup>, and friction loss is reduced by Christiansen’s F(n) factor to account for flow stepping down as each emitter in the reach draws off.
keys.ip_notes_3_def: Models one fixed inlet pressure (no pump curve), one test path only (not the full field), and a 2-parameter emitter curve (set the exponent near 0 to approximate a pressure-compensating emitter). Two different ratios are reported, deliberately kept separate: q<sub>last</sub>/q<sub>avg,field</sub> is a uniformity check, shaped like textbook low-quarter Distribution Uniformity (low-group average ÷ population mean) but computed from the test lateral’s own modeled emitters, corrected by an entered Δpressure estimate rather than a full-field statistical sample — the test lateral is deliberately the presumed worst case, so its raw, uncorrected average would understate the true field average and make uniformity look better than it is; the Δpressure input exists specifically to counter that bias. Values at or above 1 are still possible (e.g. the Δpressure estimate is too small, or a favorable downhill run). q<sub>last</sub>/q<sub>design</sub> is a different, non-uniformity check against the manufacturer’s rated flow — useful for spotting an over- or under-pressured system overall, but not a substitute for the uniformity number, since the design/rated flow has no necessary relationship to the system’s actual mean operating pressure.
keys.ip_notes_4_def: Christiansen, J.E. (1942). “Irrigation by sprinkling.” California Agricultural Experiment Station Bulletin 670. ASAE/ASABE standards for microirrigation design use the same multi-outlet friction-loss approach.
keys.ip_notes_5_def: Application rate and system/zone flow use the estimated field-average emitter flow (q<sub>avg,field</sub> — the test lateral’s own average, corrected by the entered Δpressure estimate), not a guessed rate — the same math as the Drip/Sprinkler Application Rate calculator, but fed by the corrected modeled value. Spacing and system-wide lateral/emitter counts are separate inputs here because the test path only models one worst-case branch, not every lateral in the field.
keys.irr_card_pressure_desc: Model the pressure and flow profile along a main-lateral-emitter branch to estimate distribution uniformity from the real test-path pressure, not just a catalog emitter flow rate.
